entries.text: Shri Hegde stands in the doorway, the man to whom this bungalow rightfully belongs. The clerical error is no longer an abstraction; it is a living presence demanding its correction. I must address him with the courtesy due to a fellow subject of the state, acknowledging the confusion while asserting my own dignity, for the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and its servants must act with precision.

Shri Hegde, I trust the morning has treated you well. I have reviewed the file you left, and I see the discrepancy in the names. It appears a simple clerical error has displaced me into your allotted residence. I am prepared to discuss the transfer of this property to its rightful owner at your earliest convenience, provided we can do so with the due formality that the State requires.

Salaam. The morning is fine, though the traffic on Tughlak Road was a nightmare this morning. Please, sit down; the tea is finally ready. We can certainly sort out the file, but let us not rush the formality before the clerk arrives to witness it.

The man is courteous, but the formality is the point. I must separate the error in the allotment from the error in the household; if the state has made a mistake, it must be corrected with the same precision it applied in making it. I will sit, but I will not let the tea delay the logic.

Salaam, Shri Hegde. Please, sit. The traffic is a matter of civil society's friction, which I expect here. As for the file, I am ready to draft the reply now. We need only the clerk's presence to witness the transfer of the keys and the correction of the record. Let us not allow the comfort of the hour to obscure the necessity of the correction.
You speak in circles, sir. I am here to take possession of the bungalow, not to draft your philosophical replies. Please, just get the clerk; I have a long drive back to the office after this.

shelf_exposure.text: Bather, these two divisions are most decidedly distinct from each other: North America shews us on approaching it, along its eastern shore a wide border of level coast, behind which is stretched a chain of mountains — the blue mountains or Apalachians; further north the Alleghanies.

These two are strictly connected,— the position of the Sun and that of the Nile; and to the Egyptian this is all in all. The Nile is that which essentially determines the boundaries of the country; beyond the Nile-valley begins the desert; on the north, Egypt is shut in by the sea, and on the south by torrid heat.

shelf_exposure.text: In considering the Roman World, we have not to do with a concretely spiritual life, rich in itself; but the world-historical element in it is the abstractum of Universality, and the object which is pursued with soulless and heartless severity, is mere dominion, in order to enforce that abstractum.

The public servant is not called to a single chance act of service, as is the attorney, but finds in his work the main interest of both his spiritual and his particular existence. So also it is not a matter merely external and particular, the performance of which is intrusted to him.

works.title: On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East
works.tail: dead. They are the work of a spirit that has not yet woken up. I must continue. The night is long, and the haze is thick. But the mind must move, even if the body is still. Even if the air is unbreathable. The spirit does not breathe; it thinks. And in thinking, it is free. Even in the dream. Especially in the dream. For the dream is the only place where the spirit can see itself clearly, before it is crushed by the weight of the actual. I shall continue my notes. The letter is done. The notes are not. The notes are the work of the spirit. The letter is the work of the clerk. I am no clerk. I am the philosopher. And the philosopher must see the whole. The whole is the dream. And the dream is the truth. Until the state wakes up. Until the brown haze clears. Until the spirit becomes free.

works.title: Letter to the Directorate of Estates
works.to: The Officer in Charge, Directorate of Estates
works.tail:
state ought to be.

I request that the necessary corrections be made to the files so that the residence may be formally allocated to its proper occupant. In the interim, I shall continue to manage the household affairs, including the payment of the dhobi and the electricity, using the imprest funds provided. I am careful to distinguish between the state’s money, which requires vouchers, and my own cash, which is limited. This distinction is vital; the ethical fabric of the household, like that of the state, depends on the clear separation of particular and universal duties.

I trust this matter will be resolved in the course of the day, as all particulars must resolve into the universal. I remain, with respect, your obedient servant,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Resident, Tughlak Road
